items.stem: Which of the following best describes "fossil"?
options: The preserved remains or traces of an organism that lived long ago, usually found in rock
A random change in the DNA base sequence, the original source of new alleles
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium resistant to many antibiotics
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
items.answer: The preserved remains or traces of an organism that lived long ago, usually found in rock
items.markingKey: A. "fossil" is the preserved remains or traces of an organism that lived long ago, usually found in rock.

items.stem: Explain the difference between analogous structures and homologous structures.
items.answer: Homologous structures share the same underlying anatomy because of a common ancestor but may have different functions; analogous structures have the same function (e.g. wings of birds and insects) but evolved separately with different structures.
items.markingKey: Homologous structures share the same underlying anatomy because of a common ancestor but may have different functions; analogous structures have the same function (e.g. wings of birds and insects) but evolved separately with different structures. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how the fossil record of the horse provides evidence for evolution.
items.answer: Fossils in successively younger rock show gradual changes – larger body size, fewer toes, longer legs and teeth for grazing – matching adaptation to open grasslands over about 55 million years.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Fossils in successively younger rock show gradual changes – larger body size, fewer toes, longer legs and teeth for grazing – matching adaptation to open grasslands over about 55 million years. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe Tiktaalik roseae (2004) and explain what it reveals about testable predictions in evolution.
items.answer: Palaeontologists predicted that fish-to-land transitional fossils would be found in 375-million-year-old river rocks and searched Arctic Canada; they found Tiktaalik, a fish with a neck, sturdy fins and lungs. A successful prediction about where and in which age of rock a fossil would be found is strong evidence for evolution.
items.markingKey: Context (Palaeontologists predicted that fish-to-land transitional fossils would be found in 375-million-year-old river rocks and searched Arctic Canada; they found Tiktaalik, a fish with a neck, sturdy fins and lungs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A successful prediction about where and in which age of rock a fossil would be found is strong evidence for evolution. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to testable predictions in evolution.

items.stem: The DNA of a macaque differs from human DNA at 6.5% of bases; the DNA of a orang-utan differs at 3.1%. Which species is more closely related to humans, and why?
items.answer: The orang-utan; fewer differences means a more recent common ancestor
items.markingKey: 1 orang-utan; 1 fewer DNA differences (3.1%) → less time for mutations to accumulate since the common ancestor.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the depth of a rock layer in a cliff relates to the complexity of the fossils found in it. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Choose an undisturbed sedimentary cliff with permission; mark sample squares of 1 m² at 2 m depth intervals; search each square for 20 min; photograph and identify fossils with a key; record the number of species and the most complex group; repeat at three locations along the cliff; compare with published dates for the layers.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (beware of falling rocks – wear a hard hat, stay away from overhangs, check tide times and never hammer cliff faces). Model: Choose an undisturbed sedimentary cliff with permission; mark sample squares of 1 m² at 2 m depth intervals; search each square for 20 min; photograph and identify fossils with a key; record the number of species and the most complex group; repeat at three locations along the cliff; compare with published dates for the layers.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A reduced structure that no longer has its original function, e.g. the human appendix or whale pelvic bones"?
items.answer: vestigial structure
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of vestigial structure.

items.stem: A student claims: "There are no transitional fossils." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Many transitional fossils exist, such as Archaeopteryx (dinosaurs to birds) and Tiktaalik (fish to tetrapods).
items.markingKey: Many transitional fossils exist, such as Archaeopteryx (dinosaurs to birds) and Tiktaalik (fish to tetrapods). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Ana compared the amino acid sequence of the protein cytochrome c in different species with the human sequence; three databases were used for each species and gave slightly different counts.

Time since common ancestor with humans / million years | Amino acid differences: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
90 | 4 | 4 | 4
170 | 7 | 7 | 7
310 | 13 | 13 | 13
450 | 18 | 18 | 18
600 | 23 | 23 | 24

State the time since common ancestor with humans at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 600 million years; range = 1; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 600 million years; 1 range = max − min = 24 − 23 = 1; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Describe three different types of evidence for evolution and explain how each supports the idea that species share common ancestors.
items.answer: Fossils: rock layers show a sequence of changing forms and transitional fossils (Archaeopteryx); anatomical: homologous structures (pentadactyl limb) with the same bone plan modified for different uses, vestigial structures; molecular: DNA/protein sequences – the more similar, the more recent the common ancestor; patterns from each type of evidence agree with each other.
items.markingKey: Fossils: rock layers show a sequence of changing forms and transitional fossils (Archaeopteryx); anatomical: homologous structures (pentadactyl limb) with the same bone plan modified for different uses, vestigial structures; molecular: DNA/protein sequences – the more similar, the more recent the common ancestor; patterns from each type of evidence agree with each other.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "adaptation"?
options: An inherited feature that increases an organism’s chance of survival and reproduction in its environment
The two-part scientific name of a species: genus then species, e.g. Homo sapiens
The highest rank: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya
A structure with the same basic bone arrangement in different species, showing a common ancestor, e.g. the pentadactyl limb
items.answer: An inherited feature that increases an organism’s chance of survival and reproduction in its environment
items.markingKey: A. "adaptation" is an inherited feature that increases an organism’s chance of survival and reproduction in its environment.

items.stem: Explain why natural selection does not produce a “perfect” organism.
items.answer: It can only act on existing variation; environments change; and features are trade-offs, so organisms are only better suited to current conditions than others.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It can only act on existing variation; environments change; and features are trade-offs, so organisms are only better suited to current conditions than others. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between natural selection and selective breeding.
items.answer: In natural selection the environment determines which individuals reproduce; in selective (artificial) breeding humans choose which individuals reproduce for desired traits.
items.markingKey: In natural selection the environment determines which individuals reproduce; in selective (artificial) breeding humans choose which individuals reproduce for desired traits. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Chloé plans to investigate how the colour of a background affects the survival of coloured “prey” (pasta or paper shapes) picked by student “predators”, as a model of natural selection. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: number of each colour of prey (50); size and shape of prey; collecting time (30 s); the same predators, picking one at a time
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: number of each colour of prey (50) – percentages must be comparable; size and shape of prey – larger prey are easier to find; collecting time (30 s) – longer times collect more; the same predators, picking one at a time – technique affects collection. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: "Organisms evolve because they need to adapt." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Variation arises randomly by mutation; the environment then selects individuals that already have useful variations – there is no intention.
items.markingKey: Variation arises randomly by mutation; the environment then selects individuals that already have useful variations – there is no intention. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In a sample of 200, 50 were snails with banded shells. Twenty generations later a sample of 200 contained 120 snails with banded shells. Calculate the change in percentage and explain it using natural selection.
items.answer: from 25% to 60% – an increase of 35 percentage points; the trait gave a survival advantage so more of these individuals reproduced and passed on the allele
items.markingKey: M1 50/200 = 25% and 120/200 = 60%; A1 +35 percentage points; B1 selection pressure gives advantage; B1 survivors reproduce and pass on alleles.

items.stem: Jonas plans an investigation into how the colour of a background affects the survival of coloured “prey” (pasta or paper shapes) picked by student “predators”, as a model of natural selection. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (colour of the background (green grass, brown soil, white sheet)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: "Darwin’s theory of natural selection is “just a theory” and should be taught alongside alternatives in science lessons." Discuss.
items.answer: Natural selection is a robust scientific theory; non-scientific alternatives belong in other subjects, not science.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: students should understand how ideas compete. Arguments against: in science “theory” means a well-tested explanation supported by huge evidence; alternatives such as creationism are not testable scientific explanations. Supported judgement: Natural selection is a robust scientific theory; non-scientific alternatives belong in other subjects, not science. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Explain how the dark form of the peppered moth became more common in industrial England.
items.answer: Soot darkened tree bark; pale moths were seen and eaten by birds more often; dark moths survived and reproduced more, passing on the allele for dark colour, so its frequency increased.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Soot darkened tree bark; pale moths were seen and eaten by birds more often; dark moths survived and reproduced more, passing on the allele for dark colour, so its frequency increased. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between selective breeding and natural selection.
items.answer: In natural selection the environment determines which individuals reproduce; in selective (artificial) breeding humans choose which individuals reproduce for desired traits.
items.markingKey: In natural selection the environment determines which individuals reproduce; in selective (artificial) breeding humans choose which individuals reproduce for desired traits. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Isabel analysed data on the percentage of dark peppered moths caught in traps near an industrial city in different years (three trap sites).

Year | Dark moths / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1970 | 89 | 84 | 83
1980 | 49 | 51 | 52
1990 | 29 | 29 | 29
2000 | 17 | 17 | 17
2010 | 10 | 11 | 11

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The percentage of dark moths fell steadily from about 90% in 1970 to a low value by 2010. After clean-air laws, soot no longer darkened tree bark; pale moths were better camouflaged, so birds ate more dark moths and the dark allele became less common.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The percentage of dark moths fell steadily from about 90% in 1970 to a low value by 2010.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: After clean-air laws, soot no longer darkened tree bark; pale moths were better camouflaged, so birds ate more dark moths and the dark allele became less common.

items.stem: Briefly describe Peppered moth (Biston betularia) and explain what it reveals about directional selection.
items.answer: Dark moths rose to about 98% of the Manchester population by 1895; after clean-air laws, pale moths became common again. The change reversing as soot disappeared strengthened the link between camouflage and survival.
items.markingKey: Context (Dark moths rose to about 98% of the Manchester population by 1895; after clean-air laws, pale moths became common again.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The change reversing as soot disappeared strengthened the link between camouflage and survival. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to directional selection.

items.stem: Which is an example of behavioural isolation?
options: Two bird populations with different courtship songs no longer mate
items.answer: Two bird populations with different courtship songs no longer mate
items.markingKey: D. Mating signals differ.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a population and a species.
items.answer: A species is all organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring; a population is the members of one species living in a particular area.
items.markingKey: A species is all organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring; a population is the members of one species living in a particular area. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "If two animals can mate, they must be the same species." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Different species sometimes mate, but the hybrids are usually infertile, as with mules and ligers.
items.markingKey: Different species sometimes mate, but the hybrids are usually infertile, as with mules and ligers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Zara plans to investigate how isolation affects the variation in shell banding between snail populations on islands of different distances from the mainland. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: sample size (100 snails per site); habitat type sampled (hedgerow); time of year; same classification rule for “banded”
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: sample size (100 snails per site) – small samples give unreliable percentages; habitat type sampled (hedgerow) – background affects selection; time of year – snail activity changes; same classification rule for “banded” – judgement must be consistent. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Noah studied fruit flies kept on two different foods (maltose or starch) for many generations and measured the percentage of matings between flies from the same food group (three trials per generation count).

Generations apart | Same-group matings / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
5 | 57 | 60 | 57
10 | 64 | 64 | 64
20 | 74 | 69 | 72
30 | 75 | 73 | 78
40 | 78 | 81 | 79

Calculate the percentage change in the mean same-group matings between 5 and 40.
items.markingKey: M1 means 58.0 and 79.3; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 +36.8% (increase).

items.stem: Using the example of squirrels separated by the Grand Canyon (Abert’s and Kaibab squirrels), explain how geographical isolation can lead to speciation.
items.answer: One original population split by the canyon; no interbreeding (no gene flow); random mutations differ in each population; different environments (vegetation, predators, climate) give different selection pressures; natural selection changes allele frequencies (e.g. Kaibab has white tail and dark belly); over many generations differences accumulate until they could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring – separate species (currently considered subspecies, showing the process in progress).
items.markingKey: One original population split by the canyon; no interbreeding (no gene flow); random mutations differ in each population; different environments (vegetation, predators, climate) give different selection pressures; natural selection changes allele frequencies (e.g. Kaibab has white tail and dark belly); over many generations differences accumulate until they could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring – separate species (currently considered subspecies, showing the process in progress).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The formation of new species when populations become reproductively isolated and evolve differently"?
items.answer: speciation
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of speciation.

items.stem: Explain how a river changing course could lead to two new species of snail.
items.answer: The river splits the population (geographical isolation); no gene flow; different mutations and selection pressures on each side change allele frequencies; eventually the populations cannot interbreed – reproductive isolation – two species.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The river splits the population (geographical isolation); no gene flow; different mutations and selection pressures on each side change allele frequencies; eventually the populations cannot interbreed – reproductive isolation – two species. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which Cichlid fish of Lake Victoria shows rapid speciation.
items.answer: Hundreds of cichlid species evolved in the lake in about 15 000 years, with different jaws and colours; female choice of male colour keeps species apart. Shows how sexual selection and different niches drive speciation; introduced Nile perch and pollution have since caused many extinctions.
items.markingKey: Context (Hundreds of cichlid species evolved in the lake in about 15 000 years, with different jaws and colours; female choice of male colour keeps species apart.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Shows how sexual selection and different niches drive speciation; introduced Nile perch and pollution have since caused many extinctions. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to rapid speciation.

items.stem: Elena plans an investigation into how isolation affects the variation in shell banding between snail populations on islands of different distances from the mainland. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (distance of the island from the mainland (km)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: In the name Panthera leo, what does Panthera represent?
items.answer: The genus
items.markingKey: D. The genus is written first with a capital.

items.stem: The cat is Felis catus and the domestic dog is Canis familiaris. What do the names tell you?
options: They are in the same genus
They are in the same species
items.answer: They are in different genera
items.markingKey: D. B1 the first word is the genus – they are in different genera.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a species and a genus.
items.answer: A genus is a group of closely related species; a species is a single group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
items.markingKey: A genus is a group of closely related species; a species is a single group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Ana compared the percentage of shared DNA between humans and other species in the same and different taxonomic groups (kingdom only = 1 … same genus = 7; three published estimates each).

Number of shared taxonomic ranks | DNA similarity / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 71 | 70 | 69
3 | 86 | 80 | 87
4 | 88 | 94 | 92
5 | 97 | 102 | 98
6 | 105 | 110 | 106

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: DNA similarity increases the more taxonomic ranks two species share. Species that share lower ranks (family, genus) share a more recent common ancestor, so there has been less time for DNA differences to accumulate.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: DNA similarity increases the more taxonomic ranks two species share.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Species that share lower ranks (family, genus) share a more recent common ancestor, so there has been less time for DNA differences to accumulate.

items.stem: With reference to Carl Woese and the three domains (1977–1990), explain how it illustrates molecular classification.
items.answer: By comparing ribosomal RNA sequences, Woese found that some “bacteria” were very different and proposed the domain Archaea. Molecular data overturned the two-group prokaryote/eukaryote view of life.
items.markingKey: Context (By comparing ribosomal RNA sequences, Woese found that some “bacteria” were very different and proposed the domain Archaea.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Molecular data overturned the two-group prokaryote/eukaryote view of life. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to molecular classification.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the number of features in a dichotomous key affects how accurately students identify leaf species. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): some leaves (e.g. yew) are toxic – wash hands; avoid plants with thorns or irritant sap. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. some leaves (e.g. yew) are toxic – wash hands; avoid plants with thorns or irritant sap); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The two-part scientific name of a species: genus then species, e.g. Homo sapiens"?
items.answer: binomial name
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of binomial name.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a dichotomous key must use features that do not vary within a species.
items.answer: If a feature varies (e.g. size or colour in individuals), the same species could be sent down different branches and misidentified.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If a feature varies (e.g. size or colour in individuals), the same species could be sent down different branches and misidentified. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Bacteria and archaea are basically the same." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Archaea differ from bacteria in membrane lipids, cell walls and genes, and are as different from bacteria as we are; they are a separate domain.
items.markingKey: Archaea differ from bacteria in membrane lipids, cell walls and genes, and are as different from bacteria as we are; they are a separate domain. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write a dichotomous key to separate five animals: spider, butterfly, earthworm, snail, crab. Explain why each question uses a fixed, observable feature.
items.answer: e.g. 1 Legs present? yes → 2; no → 4. 2 Eight legs? yes → spider; no → 3. 3 Wings? yes → butterfly; no (10 legs, hard shell) → crab. 4 Shell present? yes → snail; no → earthworm. Fixed features (number of legs, presence of wings/shell) do not vary between individuals of a species or with age, so identification is reliable; avoid size or colour.
items.markingKey: e.g. 1 Legs present? yes → 2; no → 4. 2 Eight legs? yes → spider; no → 3. 3 Wings? yes → butterfly; no (10 legs, hard shell) → crab. 4 Shell present? yes → snail; no → earthworm. Fixed features (number of legs, presence of wings/shell) do not vary between individuals of a species or with age, so identification is reliable; avoid size or colour.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The ability of bacteria to survive an antibiotic that would normally kill them"?
items.answer: antibiotic resistance
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of antibiotic resistance.

items.stem: A student claims: "People become resistant to antibiotics." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It is the bacteria that become resistant, not the person.
items.markingKey: It is the bacteria that become resistant, not the person. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the type of antibiotic affects the growth of a harmless bacterium (E. coli K-12) on agar plates, state the dependent variable and describe how Hana should measure it.
items.answer: diameter of the clear zone around each disc after 48 h at 25 °C
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: diameter of the clear zone around each disc after 48 h at 25 °C.

items.stem: Briefly describe Alexander Fleming’s warning (1945) and explain what it reveals about predicting resistance.
items.answer: In his Nobel lecture, Fleming warned that underdosing with penicillin could make bacteria resistant; resistant Staphylococcus was common in hospitals within a decade. His warning remains relevant: misuse of antibiotics drives resistance.
items.markingKey: Context (In his Nobel lecture, Fleming warned that underdosing with penicillin could make bacteria resistant; resistant Staphylococcus was common in hospitals within a decade.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: His warning remains relevant: misuse of antibiotics drives resistance. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to predicting resistance.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Doctors should prescribe antibiotics only after a laboratory test confirms a bacterial infection."
items.answer: Testing should be standard where possible, with rapid tests and exceptions for serious illness.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: avoids unnecessary use, slowing resistance; chooses the correct antibiotic. Arguments against: tests take time – delays could be dangerous in severe infections; not all clinics have laboratories. Supported judgement: Testing should be standard where possible, with rapid tests and exceptions for serious illness.

items.stem: Explain how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic.
items.answer: Random mutation gives some bacteria resistance; the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria; resistant ones survive and reproduce rapidly with no competition, passing on the resistance gene; the population becomes mostly resistant.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Random mutation gives some bacteria resistance; the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria; resistant ones survive and reproduce rapidly with no competition, passing on the resistance gene; the population becomes mostly resistant. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Ingrid analysed hospital data on the percentage of Staphylococcus aureus samples resistant to an antibiotic in years after the drug was introduced (three hospitals).

Years after introduction | Resistant samples / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 2 | 3 | 2
4 | 12 | 11 | 11
6 | 36 | 35 | 35
8 | 59 | 59 | 61
10 | 69 | 68 | 71

Calculate the percentage change in the mean resistant samples between 2 and 10.
items.markingKey: M1 means 2.3 and 69.3; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 +2871.4% (increase).

items.stem: Antibiotic resistance has been called a “slow pandemic”. Explain how resistance develops by natural selection and evaluate three strategies to reduce it.
items.answer: Mutation → some resistant; antibiotic kills others; survivors multiply; resistance spreads, including by plasmid transfer between bacteria. Strategies: reducing prescriptions for viral infections (effective, needs public education); finishing courses and correct doses (reduces survivors); hospital hygiene/handwashing (reduces spread of MRSA); banning routine farm use; funding new antibiotics and phage therapy (slow, expensive). Combined global approach needed.
items.markingKey: Mutation → some resistant; antibiotic kills others; survivors multiply; resistance spreads, including by plasmid transfer between bacteria. Strategies: reducing prescriptions for viral infections (effective, needs public education); finishing courses and correct doses (reduces survivors); hospital hygiene/handwashing (reduces spread of MRSA); banning routine farm use; funding new antibiotics and phage therapy (slow, expensive). Combined global approach needed.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A random change in the DNA base sequence, the original source of new alleles"?
items.answer: mutation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of mutation.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "evolution".
items.answer: The gradual change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the gradual change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why did many finch species evolve on the Galápagos Islands?
items.answer: Populations on different islands faced different food sources and were isolated
items.markingKey: Populations on different islands faced different food sources and were isolated. Adaptive radiation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why classification systems have changed over time.
items.answer: New evidence, especially DNA sequences and electron microscopy, revealed relationships that differed from those based on appearance, so groups were revised.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: New evidence, especially DNA sequences and electron microscopy, revealed relationships that differed from those based on appearance, so groups were revised. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between antivirals and antibiotics.
items.answer: Antibiotics target bacterial structures such as cell walls and ribosomes; antivirals stop viruses replicating inside host cells.
items.markingKey: Antibiotics target bacterial structures such as cell walls and ribosomes; antivirals stop viruses replicating inside host cells. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Individual organisms evolve during their lifetime." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Populations evolve over generations; individuals do not change their alleles.
items.markingKey: Populations evolve over generations; individuals do not change their alleles. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between radiometric dating and relative dating of fossils.
items.answer: Relative dating orders fossils by their rock layer (lower = older); radiometric dating uses the decay of radioactive isotopes to give an age in years.
items.markingKey: Relative dating orders fossils by their rock layer (lower = older); radiometric dating uses the decay of radioactive isotopes to give an age in years. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the species concept is difficult to apply to bacteria and fossils.
items.answer: Bacteria reproduce asexually so interbreeding cannot be tested, and fossils cannot be tested for fertile offspring.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Bacteria reproduce asexually so interbreeding cannot be tested, and fossils cannot be tested for fertile offspring. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The wolf is Canis lupus and the tiger is Panthera tigris. What do the names tell you?
options: They are in the same species
They are in the same genus
items.answer: They are in different genera
items.markingKey: D. B1 the first word is the genus – they are in different genera.

items.stem: An antibiotic disc on an agar plate of bacteria produced a clear zone of diameter 12 mm. Calculate the area of the clear zone (A = πr²) and explain what a smaller zone would show.
items.answer: 113 mm²; a smaller zone shows the bacteria are less sensitive (more resistant) to the antibiotic
items.markingKey: M1 r = 6 mm; M1 π × 6²; A1 113 mm²; B1 smaller clear zone → antibiotic less effective / bacteria more resistant.

items.stem: In a sample of 400, 40 were beetles with green shells. Twenty generations later a sample of 400 contained 180 beetles with green shells. Calculate the change in percentage and explain it using natural selection.
items.answer: from 10% to 45% – an increase of 35 percentage points; the trait gave a survival advantage so more of these individuals reproduced and passed on the allele
items.markingKey: M1 40/400 = 10% and 180/400 = 45%; A1 +35 percentage points; B1 selection pressure gives advantage; B1 survivors reproduce and pass on alleles.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the depth of a rock layer in a cliff relates to the complexity of the fossils found in it, state the dependent variable and describe how Freya should measure it.
items.answer: number of different fossil species (and the most complex body plan) found per 1 m² of rock face
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: number of different fossil species (and the most complex body plan) found per 1 m² of rock face.

items.stem: Kenji is investigating how isolation affects the variation in shell banding between snail populations on islands of different distances from the mainland. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: distance of the island from the mainland (km)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: distance of the island from the mainland (km) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the number of features in a dichotomous key affects how accurately students identify leaf species, state the dependent variable and describe how Chloé should measure it.
items.answer: percentage of 20 leaf samples correctly identified
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: percentage of 20 leaf samples correctly identified.

items.stem:
Priya analysed hospital data on the percentage of Staphylococcus aureus samples resistant to an antibiotic in years after the drug was introduced (three hospitals).

Years after introduction | Resistant samples / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 3 | 3 | 3
4 | 13 | 13 | 13
6 | 42 | 26 | 41
8 | 67 | 71 | 67
10 | 79 | 82 | 77

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean resistant samples at 6, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 26 % (trial 2 at 6); mean = 41.5 %
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (26) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 41.5 %.

items.stem: Tomás wants to find out how the colour of a background affects the survival of coloured “prey” (pasta or paper shapes) picked by student “predators”, as a model of natural selection. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does colour of the background affect percentage of each colour of prey remaining after 30 s of collecting?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (colour of the background (green grass, brown soil, white sheet)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (percentage of each colour of prey remaining after 30 s of collecting) in a question form.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "DNA evidence has made fossil evidence unnecessary for understanding evolution."
items.answer: Fossils and DNA are complementary; together they give a far more complete picture than either alone.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: DNA gives precise, quantitative relationships between living species; can detect relationships invisible in anatomy. Arguments against: DNA rarely survives beyond about a million years, so extinct groups need fossils; fossils show what ancestors looked like and when changes happened. Supported judgement: Fossils and DNA are complementary; together they give a far more complete picture than either alone.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Building motorways through wild areas could eventually cause new species to form."
items.answer: Roads can isolate populations, but the main risk is local extinction, not new species; wildlife crossings help maintain gene flow.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: roads are barriers that isolate populations of small animals; different selection pressures on each side. Arguments against: speciation needs thousands of generations – far longer than road lifetimes; small isolated populations are more likely to go extinct than to speciate. Supported judgement: Roads can isolate populations, but the main risk is local extinction, not new species; wildlife crossings help maintain gene flow. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "DNA barcoding should replace dichotomous keys for identifying species."
items.answer: DNA barcoding is powerful for research and difficult cases, but keys remain useful for fieldwork.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: accurate even for similar-looking species, larvae or fragments; objective. Arguments against: needs laboratory equipment and databases; keys are cheap, quick and usable in the field. Supported judgement: DNA barcoding is powerful for research and difficult cases, but keys remain useful for fieldwork. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the type of antibiotic affects the growth of a harmless bacterium (E. coli K-12) on agar plates. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Using aseptic technique, spread E. coli K-12 evenly on nutrient agar; place four antibiotic discs and a control disc soaked in sterile water with sterile forceps; tape the lid with two strips (do not seal fully); incubate upside down at 25 °C for 48 h; measure zone diameters with a ruler; repeat with three plates.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (aseptic technique: disinfect benches, flame loops, never open incubated plates, autoclave all cultures before disposal). Model: Using aseptic technique, spread E. coli K-12 evenly on nutrient agar; place four antibiotic discs and a control disc soaked in sterile water with sterile forceps; tape the lid with two strips (do not seal fully); incubate upside down at 25 °C for 48 h; measure zone diameters with a ruler; repeat with three plates.

items.stem: Which scientist co-published the theory of natural selection with Charles Darwin in 1858?
items.answer: Alfred Russel Wallace
items.markingKey: A. Both worked independently.

items.stem: Which evidence for evolution comes from comparing cytochrome c protein sequences?
items.answer: Molecular (biochemical) evidence
items.markingKey: B. More differences → more distant relationship.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "hybrid".
items.answer: The offspring of two different species, often infertile (e.g. a mule)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the offspring of two different species, often infertile (e.g. a mule). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between natural (phylogenetic) classification and artificial classification.
items.answer: Artificial classification uses convenient features such as habitat or colour; natural classification groups organisms by evolutionary relationships using many shared features and DNA.
items.markingKey: Artificial classification uses convenient features such as habitat or colour; natural classification groups organisms by evolutionary relationships using many shared features and DNA. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between antibiotics and antivirals.
items.answer: Antibiotics target bacterial structures such as cell walls and ribosomes; antivirals stop viruses replicating inside host cells.
items.markingKey: Antibiotics target bacterial structures such as cell walls and ribosomes; antivirals stop viruses replicating inside host cells. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why Lamarck’s idea of inheritance of acquired characteristics was rejected.
items.answer: Changes during a lifetime (e.g. bigger muscles) do not alter the DNA in sex cells, so they are not passed on; experiments failed to show such inheritance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Changes during a lifetime (e.g. bigger muscles) do not alter the DNA in sex cells, so they are not passed on; experiments failed to show such inheritance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why vestigial structures support the theory of evolution.
items.answer: They are reduced remnants of structures that were useful in ancestors; they would not be expected if species were created separately with no shared history.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are reduced remnants of structures that were useful in ancestors; they would not be expected if species were created separately with no shared history. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A new species forms when one individual has a big mutation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Speciation usually involves many small changes accumulating in an isolated population over many generations.
items.markingKey: Speciation usually involves many small changes accumulating in an isolated population over many generations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "Organisms that look similar must be closely related." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Unrelated organisms can look similar due to convergent evolution, e.g. sharks and dolphins; DNA reveals true relationships.
items.markingKey: Unrelated organisms can look similar due to convergent evolution, e.g. sharks and dolphins; DNA reveals true relationships. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mateo wants to find out how the type of antibiotic affects the growth of a harmless bacterium (E. coli K-12) on agar plates. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does antibiotic on the paper disc affect diameter of the clear zone around each disc after 48 h at 25 °C?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (antibiotic on the paper disc (four types, same concentration)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (diameter of the clear zone around each disc after 48 h at 25 °C) in a question form.

items.stem:
Mohammed analysed data on the percentage of dark peppered moths caught in traps near an industrial city in different years (three trap sites).

Year | Dark moths / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1970 | 108 | 102 | 107
1980 | 62 | 60 | 61
1990 | 37 | 36 | 36
2000 | 22 | 21 | 22
2010 | 13 | 13 | 14

Calculate the mean dark moths when the year was 1980.
items.markingKey: M1 (62 + 60 + 61) ÷ 3; A1 61.0 % (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem:
Diego compared the amino acid sequence of the protein cytochrome c in different species with the human sequence; three databases were used for each species and gave slightly different counts.

Time since common ancestor with humans / million years | Amino acid differences: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
90 | 3 | 3 | 3
170 | 6 | 4 | 6
310 | 11 | 10 | 10
450 | 14 | 15 | 15
600 | 19 | 20 | 20

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean amino acid differences at 170 million years, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 4 (trial 2 at 170 million years); mean = 6.0
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (4) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 6.0.

items.stem:
Felix studied fruit flies kept on two different foods (maltose or starch) for many generations and measured the percentage of matings between flies from the same food group (three trials per generation count).

Generations apart | Same-group matings / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
5 | 57 | 57 | 56
10 | 62 | 65 | 61
20 | 71 | 71 | 72
30 | 76 | 76 | 76
40 | 73 | 74 | 77

Calculate the mean same-group matings when the generations apart was 20.
items.markingKey: M1 (71 + 71 + 72) ÷ 3; A1 71.3 % (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem:
Rafael compared the percentage of shared DNA between humans and other species in the same and different taxonomic groups (kingdom only = 1 … same genus = 7; three published estimates each).

Number of shared taxonomic ranks | DNA similarity / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 60 | 64 | 60
3 | 76 | 77 | 72
4 | 82 | 85 | 82
5 | 91 | 90 | 91
6 | 95 | 95 | 99

Calculate the mean DNA similarity when the number of shared taxonomic ranks was 1.
items.markingKey: M1 (60 + 64 + 60) ÷ 3; A1 61.3 % (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: With reference to Global antimicrobial resistance (2019), explain how it illustrates scale of the problem.
items.answer: A major study estimated about 1.27 million deaths in 2019 were directly caused by antibiotic-resistant infections. The WHO lists resistance among the top global public-health threats.
items.markingKey: Context (A major study estimated about 1.27 million deaths in 2019 were directly caused by antibiotic-resistant infections.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The WHO lists resistance among the top global public-health threats. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to scale of the problem.

items.stem: Briefly describe Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos and explain what it reveals about natural selection measured in the wild.
items.answer: Peter and Rosemary Grant showed that after the 1977 drought, finches with larger, deeper beaks survived better because only large, hard seeds were left; the next generation had larger average beaks. It showed natural selection can change a population measurably in a single generation.
items.markingKey: Context (Peter and Rosemary Grant showed that after the 1977 drought, finches with larger, deeper beaks survived better because only large, hard seeds were left; the next generation had larger average beaks.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It showed natural selection can change a population measurably in a single generation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to natural selection measured in the wild.

items.stem: Maya investigated how isolation affects the variation in shell banding between snail populations on islands of different distances from the mainland. The method had this weakness: different habitats were sampled on each island. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: sample the same habitat type everywhere so background colour is controlled
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: sample the same habitat type everywhere so background colour is controlled

items.stem: "DNA barcoding should replace dichotomous keys for identifying species." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: DNA barcoding is powerful for research and difficult cases, but keys remain useful for fieldwork.

items.stem: "Doctors should prescribe antibiotics only after a laboratory test confirms a bacterial infection." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Testing should be standard where possible, with rapid tests and exceptions for serious illness.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: avoids unnecessary use, slowing resistance; chooses the correct antibiotic. Arguments against: tests take time – delays could be dangerous in severe infections; not all clinics have laboratories. Supported judgement: Testing should be standard where possible, with rapid tests and exceptions for serious illness.
